title: 2 Samuel 15:13–23
context: When word comes that Israel's hearts have turned to Absalom, David decides to flee Jerusalem rather than fight in the city. He leaves ten concubines behind and departs with his household and loyal soldiers, including foreign mercenaries. Ittai the Gittite, a recent arrival, refuses to turn back and pledges loyalty to David in life or death. The whole land weeps as the king crosses the brook Kidron toward the wilderness.

verses.text: A messenger came to David, saying, “The hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom.”
verses.arminianNotes: "The hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom." Arminian readers see the result of Absalom's deliberate campaign and the people's real choices, a grief-filled moment of national division.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in the report the beginning of the discipline Nathan foretold. Psalm 3, headed “A Psalm by David, when he fled from Absalom his son,” shows David turning to God in this crisis.

verses.text: David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, “Arise! Let’s flee, or else none of us will escape from Absalom. Hurry to depart, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down evil on us, and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”
verses.arminianNotes: David orders an immediate flight to spare Jerusalem. Arminian readers see a king choosing to protect the city and people rather than cling to power, a costly but wise decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David does not fight for his throne by force but entrusts himself to God. His flight spares the city and leaves the outcome in God's hands, as verse 25 will show.

verses.text: The king’s servants said to the king, “Behold, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king chooses.”
verses.arminianNotes: The servants are ready to do whatever the king chooses. Arminian readers see loyalty freely given in a crisis, a contrast to the hearts Absalom stole through flattery and deception.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God preserves faithful servants for David even when many turn away. Their loyalty is a quiet sign that David's kingship has not been abandoned by God.

verses.text: The king went out, and all his household after him. The king left ten women, who were concubines, to keep the house.
verses.arminianNotes: David leaves ten concubines to keep the house. Arminian readers note this detail without comment for now, but it sets up the painful fulfillment in 16:21–22, where Absalom shames them publicly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this detail prepares for the fulfillment of 12:11, where God said David's wives would be taken "in the sight of this sun." The narrator quietly places the pieces of the judgment.

verses.text: The king went out, and all the people after him; and they stayed in Beth Merhak.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and the people go out and pause at Beth Merhak, a name often taken to mean "far house." Arminian readers see a king who leads from among the people, sharing their hardship rather than separating himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the solemn pacing of the exodus from Jerusalem. The king God chose is leaving his city, and the narrative invites readers to feel the weight of God's discipline on David.

verses.text: All his servants passed on beside him; and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men who came after him from Gath, passed on before the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The Cherethites, Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites from Gath pass before the king. Arminian readers note that foreigners stand loyal while many Israelites defect, a striking reversal of expectations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing protection through unexpected allies. Men from Gath, Goliath's city, now guard Israel's king, a sign that God's purposes reach beyond Israel's own people.

verses.text: Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why do you also go with us? Return, and stay with the king; for you are a foreigner and also an exile. Return to your own place.
verses.arminianNotes: David urges Ittai, "a foreigner and also an exile," to return. Arminian readers see David's generosity: he will not demand loyalty from a newcomer who has no obligation to share his danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note David's humility in calling Absalom "the king" in this speech. Even in flight, David refuses to grasp at power and frees others from bearing his burden.

verses.text: Whereas you came but yesterday, should I today make you go up and down with us, since I go where I may? Return, and take back your brothers. Mercy and truth be with you.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Mercy and truth be with you." Arminian readers see David blessing Ittai with covenant language, wishing God's steadfast love and faithfulness on a foreigner who has shown him kindness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that "mercy and truth" echo God's covenant character. David, in his own distress, prays God's faithful love over a Gentile, a glimpse of God's grace extending beyond Israel.

verses.text: Ittai answered the king and said, “As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, surely in what place my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, your servant will be there also.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ittai swears, "whether for death or for life, your servant will be there also." Arminian readers see a freely chosen loyalty that recalls Ruth's pledge to Naomi, faith expressed in costly commitment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear echoes of Ruth's devotion and see God raising up a faithful foreigner. Ittai's oath by the LORD shows that he has come to trust Israel's God, not merely Israel's king.

verses.text: David said to Ittai, “Go and pass over.” Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones who were with him.
verses.arminianNotes: David lets Ittai pass over with his men and their little ones. Arminian readers see loyalty honored and received, as David accepts the commitment Ittai has freely offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that whole families now join David's flight. God gathers a faithful company around his king, a community formed by loyalty in the time of trouble.

verses.text: All the country wept with a loud voice, and all the people passed over. The king also himself passed over the brook Kidron, and all the people passed over toward the way of the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: "All the country wept with a loud voice" as the king crosses the Kidron. Arminian readers see a moment of national grief over the consequences of sin, both David's and Absalom's.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Kidron is later crossed by Jesus on the night of his betrayal (John 18:1). Many see a parallel between the rejected king leaving Jerusalem and the greater Son of David, though the text does not state it.
